notes: Weekly Career Missions. Each week a student gets one mission, chosen from the ones that fit their results (top career matches, year level, state, study preference) and rotated so they don't repeat soon.

Placeholders filled from the student's results: {career}, {careerLower}, {course}, {provider}, {atar}, {tafeCourse}, {tafeProvider}, {pathway}, {admissionsCentre}, {admissionsUrl}, {pay}, {employed}, {challenge}, {project}, {family}.

requires: course (a university course is listed for the career), tafe (a TAFE course is listed), jsa (JSA profile figures), challenge (a skill to build), lead (university or tafe: the student's preferred kind of study), years (year levels).
Effort sets the points: quick 50, standard 75, stretch 100. Students under 18 are always told to arrange contact with adults through a parent, carer or teacher.

missions.title: Interview someone who works as a {careerLower}
missions.why: People who do the job can tell you what a normal day is really like, which no website can.
steps: Ask a parent, carer, teacher or your careers adviser if they know someone who works as a {careerLower}. Always arrange it through an adult you trust.
Write three questions, e.g. What does a normal day look like? What surprised you about the job? What would you do at my age if you were starting again?
Have a 10 to 15 minute chat in person, by phone or on a video call.
Write down the most useful thing you heard.

missions.title: Talk to your careers adviser about {career}
missions.why: Your careers adviser knows the subjects, programs and people at your school that can help you get started.
steps: Open your results and pick the career you most want to know more about: {career}.
Book a time or drop in to see your careers adviser.
Ask about subjects, work experience and any upcoming events for this career.
Note one next step you agreed on.

missions.title: Watch a day in the life of a {careerLower}
missions.why: Seeing the real tasks helps you tell whether you'd enjoy the work, not just the idea of it.
steps: Search for "day in the life {careerLower} Australia" and watch one or two short videos.
List three tasks you would enjoy.
List one task you think you wouldn't enjoy, and why.

missions.title: Check the numbers for {career}
missions.why: Pay, hours and how many jobs there are make a real difference to everyday life.
steps: Open "The job in numbers" for {career} on your results. About {employed} people do this work, and median full-time pay is {pay}.
Look at the part-time rate and the qualifications people in the job hold.
Write one sentence on whether this fits the life you want.

missions.title: Look into {course} at {provider}
missions.why: Knowing the entry requirements early means you can choose the right subjects and avoid surprises in Year 12.
steps: Find {course} at {provider} on the Explore Uni & TAFE tab (the ATAR listed is {atar}).
Check the prerequisites and assumed knowledge, how long it takes and whether it includes placements.
Find one other university offering a similar course and compare the two.
Write down which you would put first, and why.

missions.title: Find out how to start {tafeCourse}
missions.why: Many trade and vocational careers can start while you're still at school.
steps: Read the entry requirements for {tafeCourse} at {tafeProvider} on the Explore Uni & TAFE tab.
Find out whether it's offered as an apprenticeship or traineeship, and whether you could start part of it at school (VET in schools).
Check whether fee-free TAFE places apply in your state.
Note anything you'd need to do before applying.

missions.title: Ask about a school-based apprenticeship for {career}
missions.why: A school-based apprenticeship or traineeship lets you earn, learn and finish school at the same time.
steps: Ask your careers adviser or VET coordinator whether school-based apprenticeships or traineeships are available for {careerLower} work.
Find out what you'd need: an employer, a training provider and a timetable that works with school.
With an adult, look up an Apprenticeship Connect Australia provider near you, the free national apprenticeship service.
Write down the first step you'll take.

missions.title: Check your subjects against {course}
missions.why: Some courses need particular Year 12 subjects. Checking now gives you time to change.
steps: Open {course} at {provider} on the Explore Uni & TAFE tab and note its prerequisites and assumed knowledge.
Compare them with the subjects you're taking or planning to take.
If something's missing, write a question to ask your careers adviser (there are often bridging courses).

missions.title: Put {admissionsCentre} key dates in your calendar
missions.why: Missing an application or early-bird date can cost you a place or extra fees.
steps: Visit {admissionsCentre} and find when applications open, the early-bird closing date and the offer rounds.
Add the dates to your phone calendar with a reminder a week before each.
Check whether any course you like needs something extra, such as a portfolio, interview or test.

missions.title: Find two scholarships for studying towards {career}
missions.why: Scholarships and grants can cover fees, books, travel or accommodation, and many go unclaimed.
steps: Search the scholarships pages of two universities or TAFEs you're interested in.
Find two you could be eligible for (equity, regional, academic, sport or subject-based).
Note what each one needs and when it closes.

missions.title: Build one skill for {career}
missions.why: Small, regular practice is the fastest way to grow a skill, and it gives you something real to put in your portfolio.
steps: Your results said: {challenge}
Pick one small way to practise this week, such as a school club, a free online course or a task at home.
Spend at least 30 minutes on it.
Write what you did and what you'd do next time.

missions.title: Try a mini project a {careerLower} might do
missions.why: Doing a small version of the work is one of the best ways to find out if you like it.
steps: This week's project: {project}
Spend about an hour on it.
Take a photo or keep what you made, and add it to your Skills Evidence Portfolio.

missions.title: Add evidence to your Skills Evidence Portfolio
missions.why: Writing down what you've done while it's fresh makes CVs, applications and interviews much easier later.
steps: Think of something from the last month at school, in sport, at work or volunteering.
Add it to your Skills Evidence Portfolio: what you did, what came of it and the skills it shows.
Tag at least one skill that a {careerLower} uses.

missions.title: Check {career} against what matters to you
missions.why: A job that fits your values is one you're more likely to stick with and enjoy.
steps: Look at your Career DNA and write down the three things that matter most to you in work.
For each one, note how well {career} fits it.
Write one thing you'd want to check before deciding.

missions.title: Find a career next door to {career}
missions.why: Careers in the same area often use similar skills, and one might suit you even better.
steps: Open the Careers browser and filter by {family}.
Pick one career you haven't looked at before and read about it.
Write one thing it has in common with {career} and one way it's different.

missions.title: Plan work experience in {careerLower} work
missions.why: A few days in a real workplace tells you more than any amount of reading, and it looks great on a CV.
steps: Ask your careers adviser how work experience works at your school and when it runs.
With a parent or carer, list three local workplaces where {careerLower}s work.
Draft a short, polite email asking about work experience, and have an adult check it before you send it.

missions.title: Find a volunteering role that builds skills for {career}
missions.why: Volunteering builds real skills, shows employers you're reliable and helps your community.
steps: With a parent or carer, look for volunteering through your school, local council, sports club or a charity.
Choose one that uses skills a {careerLower} needs, such as working with people, organising or hands-on work.
Find out how to sign up, and note the first date you could start.

missions.title: Plan a visit to {provider}
missions.why: Visiting, even virtually, helps you picture yourself studying there.
steps: Find {provider}'s next open day, campus tour or virtual tour (many run all year).
Write three questions to ask, e.g. about {course}, placements or student support.
Add the date to your calendar, or take the virtual tour this week.

missions.title: Ask a student what studying for {career} is like
missions.why: Current students give an honest picture of workload, placements and student life.
steps: Find a current uni or TAFE student: an older sibling, a former student from your school or a university's student ambassador chat.
Ask what a normal week looks like, what's hardest and what they wish they'd known in Year {year}.
Write down one tip you'll use.

missions.title: Find out how {career} is changing
missions.why: Jobs change with technology and demand. Knowing how helps you build the right skills.
steps: Read the job outlook and AI notes for {career} on your results.
Find one recent news article about the job in Australia.
Write one way the job might be different by 2035, and one skill that will matter more.

projects.health: Learn the DRSABCD first aid action plan and talk a family member through it.
projects.care: Plan a small, kind activity for someone in your community, such as helping an older neighbour, and write how you'd make it inclusive.
projects.education: Prepare and teach a 10-minute lesson on something you know well to a sibling, friend or family member.
projects.tech: Build a simple web page or small program that solves a problem you have, using a free online tutorial.
projects.data: Collect some data about your week (sleep, screen time or spending), make a chart and write what it shows.
projects.engineering: Design and build a small structure, such as a paper bridge, and test how much weight it holds.
projects.built: Sketch a floor plan of your bedroom to scale and redesign it to work better.
projects.environment: Do a 30-minute litter or biodiversity count in a local park and record what you find.
projects.science: Design and run a simple experiment at home, record your method and results, and write a conclusion.
projects.animals: Research the care needs of a common pet or local native animal and make a one-page care guide.
projects.business: Come up with a small business idea, work out costs and price, and write a one-page plan.
projects.creative: Make a poster, short video or design for a cause you care about, and ask for feedback.
projects.performing: Prepare and record a short performance, then watch it back and note two things to improve.
projects.trades: Help with a repair or maintenance job at home with an adult, following the safety steps.
projects.workshop: Make or fix something by hand from a plan or instructions, and note the tools and steps.
projects.hospitality: Plan, budget and cook a meal for your household, timing each dish to be ready together.
projects.safety: Make a home emergency plan with your family: exits, a meeting place and emergency numbers.
projects.fitness: Design a safe, beginner-friendly 20-minute workout and try it with a friend or family member.
projects.transport: Plan a trip across your city or region by public transport, comparing time, cost and connections.
projects.agriculture: Grow something from seed (herbs, vegetables or a seedling) and keep a short log of watering, sunlight and growth.
projects.retail: Plan a display for a product you like: who it's for, where it goes in a shop, the price and how you'd show it off.
projects.office: Organise a real task for your household or a club: a schedule, budget or shared document that others can use.
projects.manufacturing: Pick an everyday product and map how it's made, step by step, from raw materials to the shop shelf.
